Whistleblower Gamechanger

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Risking life and limb to blow the whistle on corruption and abuse of power, South Africans who want come forward, can now do so safely.

Unique Selling Point:
Surveys since 2007 by the Open Democracy Advice Centre in Cape Town and private organisations like PWC have shown that only 3 out of 10 South Africans believe the law will protect them if they blew the whistle and so there's been a steady decline in the number of people willing to shed the light on corruption. Despite 15 years of having a Protected Disclosures Act meant to protect them, whistleblowers still sacrifice everything to come forward.

Three initiatives aim to change that.

The first is by Parliament. Realising that the heroes of democracy find themselves in the cold after standing up in defence of truth, and that information brought to light seldom leads to change or the perpetrators being fired and prosecuted, Parliament has written the Public Disclosures Amendment Bill, which has this week been debated in the Parliamentary Justice Committee after a long period of public submissions. The Amendment Bill places a positive OBLIGATION on organisations to grab the bull by the horns when information on corruption and abuse it brought to light. The Amendment will put the power and security back in the hands of the whistleblower, even if the purse is on the side of their employer. We speak to Justice Committee chairperson Dr Mathole Motshekga about the mini policy revolution he's overseeing to plug the holes in policy.

Second initiative is an online whistleblowing platform developed in Australia and adopted by independent civil rights groups OUTA (Organisation Undoing Tax Abuse). Not only is OUTA's platform hacker proof and stripes out user data to protect the anonymity of submissions, but it has been designed to elicit information in a particularly helpful. detailed way that will allow the organisation to take legal action against individuals perpetrating fraud and corruption. It's a true game-changer for whistleblowers who usually walk the road of coming forward alone and risk losing their livelihoods and sometimes even their lives. OUTA will follow their cases every step of the way and make sure that perpetrators are made examples of. Using the example of Zwai Sokupa (who is speaking to us on condition of anonymity) we show how his information is enabling OUTA to blow the lid off corruption in a key development parastatal, and how they will continue to support whistleblowers financially and legally who help them reach their aim of safeguarding taxpayers' money.

But OUTA's initiative is limited to the parastatals where their investigations are focused -- for the moment ESKOM and SAA, although this will change as they get good information on other state owned enterprises. So the broader legal landscape still remains crucial to challenge, as the Amendment Bill will do -- to afford whistelblowers true protection.

So, the final initiative is by the Open Democracy Advice Centre itself -- the NGO that's been working with whistleblowers since the dawn of democracy and that's been working to change policy through research and advocacy, because it believes effective whistleblowing mechanisms are a key part of good governance. ODAC counsels and guides whistleblowers who come forward to bodies like Corruption Watch or the Public Protector, to guide them through the complex legal, emotional, psychological and often physically hazardous process of blowing the whistle. Now, hoping to take whistleblowing to the next level, and making the new law practical, helping to implement it, ODAC is launching a CODE of good practice and taking it around the country, to government departments and companies alike, to help them implement the new legislation and help make the world safe for whistleblowers.

ODAC has held the hands of families like Tlholo Phakoe's whose father Moss was gunned down in 2009 after a lengthy period of tying to raise serious corruption issues in Madibeng, North West with senior leaders of the ANC -- most notably President Zuma, whom he visited at home, with his damning dossier. The murder of Moss Phakoe remains unsolved, while COSATU and Corruption Watch still campaign behind the scenes today to have the prosecutions reopened.

It was the case of Moss Phakoe that marked a change in whistleblowing -- not only could you get fired, you could die.


Further information:
CASE STUDIES:

1. It's nearing a decade since MOSS PHAKOE was killed on 13 March 2009 after he tried to get top ANC leadership to act against fraud and corruption totalling millios of rands in the North West Province. We speak to his son Tlholoe about how his father delivered documentation to Jacob Zuma's Forest Town home and even presented info to Zuma at Nkandla. Phakoe's dossier is still being pursued by Corruption Watch and COSATU, who have not forgotten Moss' sacrifice -- we speak to COSATU Deputy Secretary General Solly Phetoe campaign to ensure that the case against the killers of the former Rustenburg municipal councillor is re-opened.

2. HIDDEN IDENTITY: We speak to Mzwandile Zwai Sokupa, the former CEO of the Construction Industry Development Board who brought to light the profligate spending of board members of the CIBD - and summarily lost his job. Zwai used every legal and available avenue to blow the whistle, but eventually had to turn to OUTA for help. Now employed elsewhere, Zwai is willing to speak, if his identity is protected, about hos OUTA's model of "walking with" whistleblowers and holding offenders to account is the only way progress will be made.

3. HIDDEN IDENTITY: Once a successful sub-contractor with a multi-million rand turn-over, for ESKOM, Martin Mpofu has lost everything and now lives in a shack after he tried to blow the whistle on unfair contracting procedures at ESKOM -- and he found his own bill going unpaid, rendering him unable to pay his workers. He's desperate for recourse and shows how vulnerable whistleblowers are

4. WENDY ADDISON spent 11 years fighting for justice after blowing the whistle on Leisurenet, the biggest corporate corruption disaster in South Africa’s history.

5. ADV MIKE TSHISHONGA After coming across what seemed to be explosive evidence of corruption and nepotism in the department’s Masters Office, of which he was managing director, Tshishonga used internal channels to report it within the framework of the Protected Disclosures Act.The PDA came into law in 2000 and encourages whistleblowing in the workplace, with the protection of the whistleblower as its focus. When months went by without any sign that his allegations – which also implicated then justice minister Penuell Maduna – Tshishonga resorted to revealing his evidence in the media, a move that would prove to have dire consequences for him. He claimed Maduna had ordered him to work with a particular liquidator in a case involving the Retail Apparel Group, despite the department’s policy stating that liquidators have to bid for contracts with the Masters Office, which selects the preferred one.

Context and need for whistleblowing: 
-    Maladministration, Corruption, Nepotism and Irregular expenditure is rapidly chipping away at the integrity, sustainability, and service delivery of our State Owned Institutions. 
-    This has become more consequential in the last few years where more and more large capital projects are being funded by Debt, rather than from treasury and tax allocations, thus the consequences are becoming more severe for the country 
-    This has been accelerating in the last few years, and more people are noticing it, not just outside, but especially inside these organisations. 
-    Many of these people in the SOE’s aren’t complicit with this behaviour, but have a feeling of helplessness because they feel isolated and afraid to speak out 

What are whistleblowers afraid of? 
-   Fear of being caught or suspected of whistleblowing or speaking out 
-    Fear of being out in the cold/storm alone 
-    They doubt the information will be used effectively, or at all by those they blow the whistle to 
-    They don’t trust the official forums and channels available to whistleblowers 
-    Reports that go into the internal channels are themselves often given to those who are guilty, exposing the whistleblower. This same scenario occurs when outside parties “facilitating” the whistleblowing on behalf of the organisation are used, since these reports still go to management, and its management that is almost invariable involved in the commission of crimes themselves in the most severe cases.  

Laws that are SUPPOSED to help whistleblowers: 
-    The protected disclosures act of 2000 
-    What it defines as “occupational detriment” and what remedies available 
-    But whistleblowers generally cannot afford to “enforce their rights” on their own, thus are disincentivised to take the risk 

How corrupt organisations (especially SOE’s) “combat” whistleblowers: 
-    Witch hunts against suspected whistleblowers when information leaks 
-    Intimidation of whistleblowers 
-    Fabrication of evidence against suspected or known whistleblowers 
-    Suspension and dismissal without proper process 
-    Appealing or ignoring findings of CCMA, knowing whistleblower doesn’t have funds to fight it in court even if they have a good case, throwing organisation’s funds behind the appeal 
-    Stretching out labour cases in effort to bankrupt whistleblower 

What would be the game changer for whistleblowers? 
-    If organisations existed that ally with whistleblowers, that enable whistleblowers to not have to stand alone in the cold after whistleblowing, who help whistleblowers weather the storm and come out on top, however long it takes. 
-    To publicly support whistleblowers where necessary, and to state whisteblower’s verified accounts successfully to the public and media (to tell the story), and to stand in defense of the whistleblower if there’s a backlash from the SOE. 
-    Organisation should have the capacity to help investigate the wrongdoing that the original whistleblowing pertains to, and prepare corruption cases against organisations and individuals responsible for corruption 
-    Prepare separate evidence against SOE for any instances of intimidation, fabrication of evidence against whistleblower, and cases of occupational detriment. 
-    Provide legal assistance to the whistleblower, and pay for direct legal costs 
-    Help recover funds owed by SOE to the whistleblower 
-    Expose both the victimising organisation and those involved in the victimisation 
-    Prepare legal cases against individuals involved in victimisation of whistleblower 
-    Prepare cases against lawyers and attorneys representing SOE that are complicit in fabrication of evidence or presenting fabricated evidence as factual. 

OUTA’s need for whistleblowers, and its willingness to fund their defence: 
-    OUTA are building larger and larger teams geared towards tackling corruption cases head on, keeping those responsible accountable to the maximum degree allowed by the law 
-    But too much time and resources are spent trying to get and mature “hidden” information that would clearly expose corruption, information that’s strong enough to build legal cases around. 
-    Whistleblowers have the ability to throw these cases wide open. They often give direct access to issues that aren’t just of historic value, but that are often occurring at the moment, and could potentially still be stopped by OUTA and its lawyers (ex. SAA BnP capital deal) 
-    The funding that enables all of this comes from tens of thousands of people and businesses who have made a commitment towards finding a direct solution to corruption

Case Study:
Mike Tshishonga Whistleblower -- fired in 2003 for lifting lid on corruption in Justice Dept, now motivational speaker & activist
Alfred Motsi Whistleblower with MOSS PHAKOE
Tlholo Phakoe Son of MOSS Phakoe

Press Release:


Whistleblowers under Fire
Whistleblowers are guardians of our democracy, acting selflessly to expose corruption, self-enrichment and wrongdoing. Thanks to the bravery of these men and women, several cases have been blown wide open in recent years, ranging from bread price fixing and text book fraud, to supply chain corruption and collusion in the construction industry. But, while they may be revealing the truth, many suffer dire persecution, untold harassment and even death. Could new legislation now finally make it safer to disclose the truth? Carte Blanche meets some of the whistleblowers under fire and the law-makers working to better protect them.
FIFTEEN SECONDS
VO: We’re quick to complain about corruption, but how many of us have the courage to walk the long, painful road of a whistleblower?
TIAAN LE ROUX: Whistle-blowers in this country have a tendency to blow open places that otherwise would be invisible forever.

FIFTEEN SECONDS
VO: Where would South Africa be without whistleblowers, acting selflessly to expose corruption?
HIDDEN VOICE: I was running the risk of the worst-case scenario, being killed. But I believe someone has got to stand up and say not in my name.

TEN SECONDS
Whistleblowers – the sentries on the wall of our democracy, acting selflessly to warn us of danger — but many suffer dire persecution. Could new legislation make it safer to disclose the truth?

Script:


Whistleblower Gamechanger
“Jason” has spent nearly three years trying to defend his reputation against accusations of theft and fraud in his job as a senior manager in a national government department.
“JASON”: I was suspended within a working day of blowing the whistle.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Within one day?
“JASON”: Within one day. Colleagues at work are afraid of talking to me, even greeting me. Even on social media we can’t even comment on each other’s statuses on Facebook or anything.
DEVI: This is a story about ordinary people who stood up against corruption armed with only the truth. These South Africans weren’t afraid to take on those with power and money and they did it because they wanted to make South Africa a better place.
A storm of character assassination erupted against Jason when he reported supply chain corruption worth tens of millions of rands to the police and Public Protector. He knew the stories of whistleblowers who’ve suffered for their convictions, but he also knew the law should protect him.
“JASON”: I must say I did a lot of soul searching before I blew the whistle and I was aware that I was running the risk of the worst-case scenario, being killed. But I believe someone has got to stand up and say not in my name.
DEVI: South Africa has state of the art legislation, the Protected Disclosures Act, since 2001 but corruption is on the increase while whistleblowing is on the decrease because whistleblowers say they don’t believe they will be protected.
But who could properly thank the whistleblowers who exposed bread price collusion that was robbing the poor? (SUBTITLE: 2007, Bread Price Fixing Scandal)
Or the non-delivery of text books that left learners adrift? (SUBTITLE: 2012, Limpopo Text Book Crisis)
Tender collusion on construction projects that drained municipalities of billions? (SUBTITLE: 2010-2016, World Cup & Construction Cartels Saga)
Investigators would make little headway without solid information from insiders in the know.
TIAAN LE ROUX: Whistle-blowers in this country have a tendency to blow open places that otherwise would be invisible forever. 
Tiaan le Roux is overseeing the evolution of the Opposition to Urban Tolling Alliance into the Organisation Undoing Tax Abuse – a donor-funded civil action group that’s just launched a hacker-proof, secure, anonymous web platform for whisteblowing.
DEVI: We’ve been following the development of OUTA for years now when it was Wayne Duvenage and his dining room table and his laptop. But you’ve grown from that to a whole floor. How important have whistle-blowers been?
TIAAN LE ROUX: The whistle-blower can give you that inside view and that has been in the last few months the primary driver for the new work that we are able to take on. 
One of first whisteblowers to test-drive the Protected Disclosures Act back in 2003 was Mike Tshishonga. He was a Deputy Director General in the Justice Department who alleged a questionable relationship between liquidator Enver Motala and Minister Penuel Maduna – Mike’s big boss.
Mike said the Minister insisted Motala be appointed to one particularly lucrative liquidation. But other liquidators already on the case objected, taking the Justice Department to court and winning their case, even after the Minister appealed.
MIKE TSHISHONGA: The minister phoned and said because I didn’t help him in the case he is removing me with immediate effect so as to where you go it’s not my business. The director general will see where to put you.
DEVI: What did you say?
MIKE TSHISHONGA: I was just shocked.
Mike followed the steps of the Protected Disclosures Act, first exhausting internal avenues before going to the Public Protector and Auditor General. He saw no progress. He was sidelined to an office where no-one spoke to him and he was given no tasks. His last resort was to write a book and go to the media.
MIKE TSHISHONGA: We had a press conference where I told the whole story. Hell broke loose. I was now suspended officially.
UPSOUND PENUELL MADUNA FILM ARCHIVE CLIP: Personally I’m not bothered by Mike Tshishonga – a lousy dunderhead we inherited from our previous Bantustans and kept afloat all these years.
To this day Maduna strenuously denies that he ever pressurised Mike. He says he only pursued Motala’s appointment because SARS had asked him to do it.
Motala calls claims of nepotism unfounded, false, defamatory and criminally injurious.
Despite the pain of months in limbo and bitter public attacks, the Protected Disclosures Act did protect Mike from being sued and the Labour Court eventually ruled that he’d acted in good faith.
Whistleblower protections are only as strong as the will to respect them – in 2009 in the town of Rustenburg, no-one was considering those protections when municipal councilor Moss Phakoe was gunned down in his driveway shortly after giving ANC top brass a hefty dossier detailing municipal corruption that he’d compiled it with colleague Alfred Motsi.
ALFRED MOTSI: It ran into hundreds of millions. It was a very big document like this.
DEVI: It included evidence…
ALFRED MOTSI: Evidence, photos, statements, everything. He stood up and looked at the then mayor and said ‘hate me but don’t hurt me’. Then he started summarizing what was contained in the dossier.
TLHOLO: Two days after my father was found dead with two bullet wounds in his body.
Tlholo Phakoe identified this father’s body at the morgue.
TLHOLO PHAKOE: He died after he put up posters campaigning for the ANC 2009 municipal elections. His car was surrounded by the face of Jacob Zuma. He was still wearing the vote ANC T-shirt in the mortuary. The blood all over.
DEVI LINK: The Protected Disclosures Act was at a crossroads. Whistleblowers could lose their jobs and their lives, rendering the law ineffective.
ALFRED MOTSI: They wanted to killed me and Moss Phakoe – so Moss Phakoe was an easy target…I’m a trained soldier. Those guys followed us. Eight of my dogs were poisoned.
DEVI: All at once?
ALFRED MOTSI: One, one, one…because they wanted to access the yard. The wheels of my vehicle were loosened so I would be involved in an accident.
In 2012 Rustenburg mayor Matthew Wolmarans and his bodyguard were convicted of the murder. Two years on, their conviction and sentences were overturned on appeal when a state witness recanted, now saying police had bribed him to implicate “an innocent man”. Phakoe’s murder remains unsolved; the NPA still considering whether to investigate perjury claims against the witness.
TLHOLO PHAKOE: They cannot say no Moss Phakoe was killed by a ghost or somebody was just mistakenly passing and saw him and shoot him and just left, no.
An amendment to strengthen the Protected Disclosures Act and compel organisations to investigate is currently before Parliament’s Justice Committee.
At the Open Democracy Advice Centre or ODAC Mukelani Dimba champions law reform knowing the thing whistleblowers fear most is that nothing will happen when they speak up. 
DEVI: In South African culture generally you would find that based on our history a whistle-blower is known to be impipi.
MUKELANI DIMBA: I would say that is our immediate history, form apartheid struggle…we don’t want spies, but if you go further back into history, we use to have Inhlabamkhosi or a sentry in English. These are people that because of the position that they are holding in the village they would see trouble or danger looming and they would raise alarm and say there’s a fire approaching. So we need to go back to that kind of history where we see whistle-blower as a sentry.
ODAC’s designed a Code of Good Practice to help organisations foster a culture that honours safe disclosure. They say only 25 of 37 JSE-listed companies that have been surveyed prohibit retaliation and only 16 have created channels for confidential whistleblowing.
Many organizations that work with whistleblowers are at best able to counsel or advise…but OUTA seeks to incorporate whistleblowers like “Jason” as consultants to help mature investigations.
TIAAN LE ROUX: We decided that it’s so important that we cannot be just an organization you can disclose to. We have to be there to assist our whistleblowers.
DEVI: This is fantastic because, if whistleblowers knew they would have support you would get more and it will snowball.
TIAAN LE ROUX: That’s the idea.
Jason is anxiously waiting for his disclosures to be investigated, hoping that soon he’ll be able to pay his kids school fees again and silence family who’ve begun to say he should have just shut up.
“JASON”: I hope that I will get a job and that one day when my tombstone is unveiled, my kids will say we are proud of this man that’s resting here.
TIAAN LE ROUX: We hope that the legislation will change, we hope the technology will enable people to more easily whistleblow but we are going to need individuals to be brave in the coming years in order to be able to do this work.
ALFRED MOTSI: South Africans must be whistleblowers…if we don’t stop this rot, tomorrow when we wake up we won’t be having a country anymore.
MIKE TSHISHONGA: The greatest tragedy in this world it’s not the bad people who are doing bad things because they know what they are doing…it is the appalling silence of the good people.

Laws that are SUPPOSED to help whistleblowers: - The protected disclosures act of 2000 - What it defines as “occupational detriment” and what remedies available - But whistleblowers generally cannot afford to “enforce their rights” on their own, thus are disincentivised to take the risk How corrupt organisations (especially SOE’s) “combat” whistleblowers: - Witch hunts against suspected whistleblowers when information leaks - Intimidation of whistleblowers - Fabrication of evidence against suspected or known whistleblowers - Suspension and dismissal without proper process - Appealing or ignoring findings of CCMA, knowing whistleblower doesn’t have funds to fight it in court even if they have a good case, throwing organisation’s funds behind the appeal - Stretching out labour cases in effort to bankrupt whistleblower What would be the game changer for whistleblowers? - If organisations existed that ally with whistleblowers, that enable whistleblowers to not have to stand alone in the cold after whistleblowing, who help whistleblowers weather the storm and come out on top, however long it takes. - To publicly support whistleblowers where necessary, and to state whisteblower’s verified accounts successfully to the public and media (to tell the story), and to stand in defense of the whistleblower if there’s a backlash from the SOE. - Organisation should have the capacity to help investigate the wrongdoing that the original whistleblowing pertains to, and prepare corruption cases against organisations and individuals responsible for corruption - Prepare separate evidence against SOE for any instances of intimidation, fabrication of evidence against whistleblower, and cases of occupational detriment. - Provide legal assistance to the whistleblower, and pay for direct legal costs - Help recover funds owed by SOE to the whistleblower - Expose both the victimising organisation and those involved in the victimisation - Prepare legal cases against individuals involved in victimisation of whistleblower - Prepare cases against lawyers and attorneys representing SOE that are complicit in fabrication of evidence or presenting fabricated evidence as factual. OUTA’s need for whistleblowers, and its willingness to fund their defence: - OUTA are building larger and larger teams geared towards tackling corruption cases head on, keeping those responsible accountable to the maximum degree allowed by the law - But too much time and resources are spent trying to get and mature “hidden” information that would clearly expose corruption, information that’s strong enough to build legal cases around. - Whistleblowers have the ability to throw these cases wide open. They often give direct access to issues that aren’t just of historic value, but that are often occurring at the moment, and could potentially still be stopped by OUTA and its lawyers (ex. Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 02 November 2016 Press Release: Whistleblowers under Fire Whistleblowers are guardians of our democracy, acting selflessly to expose corruption, self-enrichment and wrongdoing. Thanks to the bravery of these men and women, several cases have been blown wide open in recent years, ranging from bread price fixing and text book fraud, to supply chain corruption and collusion in the construction industry. But, while they may be revealing the truth, many suffer dire persecution, untold harassment and even death. Could new legislation now finally make it safer to disclose the truth? Carte Blanche meets some of the whistleblowers under fire and the law-makers working to better protect them. FIFTEEN SECONDS VO: We’re quick to complain about corruption, but how many of us have the courage to walk the long, painful road of a whistleblower? TIAAN LE ROUX: Whistle-blowers in this country have a tendency to blow open places that otherwise would be invisible forever. FIFTEEN SECONDS VO: Where would South Africa be without whistleblowers, acting selflessly to expose corruption? HIDDEN VOICE: I was running the risk of the worst-case scenario, being killed. But I believe someone has got to stand up and say not in my name. TEN SECONDS Whistleblowers – the sentries on the wall of our democracy, acting selflessly to warn us of danger — but many suffer dire persecution. Could new legislation make it safer to disclose the truth? Script: Whistleblower Gamechanger “Jason” has spent nearly three years trying to defend his reputation against accusations of theft and fraud in his job as a senior manager in a national government department. “JASON”: I was suspended within a working day of blowing the whistle. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Within one day? “JASON”: Within one day. Colleagues at work are afraid of talking to me, even greeting me. Even on social media we can’t even comment on each other’s statuses on Facebook or anything. DEVI: This is a story about ordinary people who stood up against corruption armed with only the truth. These South Africans weren’t afraid to take on those with power and money and they did it because they wanted to make South Africa a better place. A storm of character assassination erupted against Jason when he reported supply chain corruption worth tens of millions of rands to the police and Public Protector. He knew the stories of whistleblowers who’ve suffered for their convictions, but he also knew the law should protect him. “JASON”: I must say I did a lot of soul searching before I blew the whistle and I was aware that I was running the risk of the worst-case scenario, being killed. But I believe someone has got to stand up and say not in my name. DEVI: South Africa has state of the art legislation, the Protected Disclosures Act, since 2001 but corruption is on the increase while whistleblowing is on the decrease because whistleblowers say they don’t believe they will be protected. But who could properly thank the whistleblowers who exposed bread price collusion that was robbing the poor? (SUBTITLE: 2007, Bread Price Fixing Scandal) Or the non-delivery of text books that left learners adrift? (SUBTITLE: 2012, Limpopo Text Book Crisis) Tender collusion on construction projects that drained municipalities of billions? (SUBTITLE: 2010-2016, World Cup & Construction Cartels Saga) Investigators would make little headway without solid information from insiders in the know. TIAAN LE ROUX: Whistle-blowers in this country have a tendency to blow open places that otherwise would be invisible forever. Tiaan le Roux is overseeing the evolution of the Opposition to Urban Tolling Alliance into the Organisation Undoing Tax Abuse – a donor-funded civil action group that’s just launched a hacker-proof, secure, anonymous web platform for whisteblowing. DEVI: We’ve been following the development of OUTA for years now when it was Wayne Duvenage and his dining room table and his laptop. But you’ve grown from that to a whole floor. How important have whistle-blowers been? TIAAN LE ROUX: The whistle-blower can give you that inside view and that has been in the last few months the primary driver for the new work that we are able to take on. One of first whisteblowers to test-drive the Protected Disclosures Act back in 2003 was Mike Tshishonga. He was a Deputy Director General in the Justice Department who alleged a questionable relationship between liquidator Enver Motala and Minister Penuel Maduna – Mike’s big boss. Mike said the Minister insisted Motala be appointed to one particularly lucrative liquidation. But other liquidators already on the case objected, taking the Justice Department to court and winning their case, even after the Minister appealed. MIKE TSHISHONGA: The minister phoned and said because I didn’t help him in the case he is removing me with immediate effect so as to where you go it’s not my business. The director general will see where to put you. DEVI: What did you say? MIKE TSHISHONGA: I was just shocked. Mike followed the steps of the Protected Disclosures Act, first exhausting internal avenues before going to the Public Protector and Auditor General. He saw no progress. He was sidelined to an office where no-one spoke to him and he was given no tasks. His last resort was to write a book and go to the media. MIKE TSHISHONGA: We had a press conference where I told the whole story. Hell broke loose. I was now suspended officially. UPSOUND PENUELL MADUNA FILM ARCHIVE CLIP: Personally I’m not bothered by Mike Tshishonga – a lousy dunderhead we inherited from our previous Bantustans and kept afloat all these years. To this day Maduna strenuously denies that he ever pressurised Mike. He says he only pursued Motala’s appointment because SARS had asked him to do it. Motala calls claims of nepotism unfounded, false, defamatory and criminally injurious. Despite the pain of months in limbo and bitter public attacks, the Protected Disclosures Act did protect Mike from being sued and the Labour Court eventually ruled that he’d acted in good faith. Whistleblower protections are only as strong as the will to respect them – in 2009 in the town of Rustenburg, no-one was considering those protections when municipal councilor Moss Phakoe was gunned down in his driveway shortly after giving ANC top brass a hefty dossier detailing municipal corruption that he’d compiled it with colleague Alfred Motsi. ALFRED MOTSI: It ran into hundreds of millions. It was a very big document like this. DEVI: It included evidence… ALFRED MOTSI: Evidence, photos, statements, everything. He stood up and looked at the then mayor and said ‘hate me but don’t hurt me’. Then he started summarizing what was contained in the dossier. TLHOLO: Two days after my father was found dead with two bullet wounds in his body. Tlholo Phakoe identified this father’s body at the morgue. TLHOLO PHAKOE: He died after he put up posters campaigning for the ANC 2009 municipal elections. His car was surrounded by the face of Jacob Zuma. He was still wearing the vote ANC T-shirt in the mortuary. The blood all over. DEVI LINK: The Protected Disclosures Act was at a crossroads. Whistleblowers could lose their jobs and their lives, rendering the law ineffective. ALFRED MOTSI: They wanted to killed me and Moss Phakoe – so Moss Phakoe was an easy target…I’m a trained soldier. Those guys followed us. Eight of my dogs were poisoned. DEVI: All at once? ALFRED MOTSI: One, one, one…because they wanted to access the yard. The wheels of my vehicle were loosened so I would be involved in an accident. In 2012 Rustenburg mayor Matthew Wolmarans and his bodyguard were convicted of the murder. Two years on, their conviction and sentences were overturned on appeal when a state witness recanted, now saying police had bribed him to implicate “an innocent man”. Phakoe’s murder remains unsolved; the NPA still considering whether to investigate perjury claims against the witness. TLHOLO PHAKOE: They cannot say no Moss Phakoe was killed by a ghost or somebody was just mistakenly passing and saw him and shoot him and just left, no. An amendment to strengthen the Protected Disclosures Act and compel organisations to investigate is currently before Parliament’s Justice Committee. At the Open Democracy Advice Centre or ODAC Mukelani Dimba champions law reform knowing the thing whistleblowers fear most is that nothing will happen when they speak up. DEVI: In South African culture generally you would find that based on our history a whistle-blower is known to be impipi. MUKELANI DIMBA: I would say that is our immediate history, form apartheid struggle…we don’t want spies, but if you go further back into history, we use to have Inhlabamkhosi or a sentry in English. These are people that because of the position that they are holding in the village they would see trouble or danger looming and they would raise alarm and say there’s a fire approaching. So we need to go back to that kind of history where we see whistle-blower as a sentry. ODAC’s designed a Code of Good Practice to help organisations foster a culture that honours safe disclosure. They say only 25 of 37 JSE-listed companies that have been surveyed prohibit retaliation and only 16 have created channels for confidential whistleblowing. Many organizations that work with whistleblowers are at best able to counsel or advise…but OUTA seeks to incorporate whistleblowers like “Jason” as consultants to help mature investigations. TIAAN LE ROUX: We decided that it’s so important that we cannot be just an organization you can disclose to. We have to be there to assist our whistleblowers. DEVI: This is fantastic because, if whistleblowers knew they would have support you would get more and it will snowball. TIAAN LE ROUX: That’s the idea. Jason is anxiously waiting for his disclosures to be investigated, hoping that soon he’ll be able to pay his kids school fees again and silence family who’ve begun to say he should have just shut up. “JASON”: I hope that I will get a job and that one day when my tombstone is unveiled, my kids will say we are proud of this man that’s resting here. TIAAN LE ROUX: We hope that the legislation will change, we hope the technology will enable people to more easily whistleblow but we are going to need individuals to be brave in the coming years in order to be able to do this work. ALFRED MOTSI: South Africans must be whistleblowers…if we don’t stop this rot, tomorrow when we wake up we won’t be having a country anymore. MIKE TSHISHONGA: The greatest tragedy in this world it’s not the bad people who are doing bad things because they know what they are doing…it is the appalling silence of the good people.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Risking life and limb to blow the whistle on corruption and abuse of power, South Africans who want come forward, can now do so safely.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Surveys since 2007 by the Open Democracy Advice Centre in Cape Town and private organisations like PWC have shown that only 3 out of 10 South Africans believe the law will protect them if they blew the whistle and so there's been a steady decline in the number of people willing to shed the light on corruption. Despite 15 years of having a Protected Disclosures Act meant to protect them, whistleblowers still sacrifice everything to come forward. Three initiatives aim to change that. The first is by Parliament. Realising that the heroes of democracy find themselves in the cold after standing up in defence of truth, and that information brought to light seldom leads to change or the perpetrators being fired and prosecuted, Parliament has written the Public Disclosures Amendment Bill, which has this week been debated in the Parliamentary Justice Committee after a long period of public submissions. The Amendment Bill places a positive OBLIGATION on organisations to grab the bull by the horns when information on corruption and abuse it brought to light. The Amendment will put the power and security back in the hands of the whistleblower, even if the purse is on the side of their employer. We speak to Justice Committee chairperson Dr Mathole Motshekga about the mini policy revolution he's overseeing to plug the holes in policy. Second initiative is an online whistleblowing platform developed in Australia and adopted by independent civil rights groups OUTA (Organisation Undoing Tax Abuse). Not only is OUTA's platform hacker proof and stripes out user data to protect the anonymity of submissions, but it has been designed to elicit information in a particularly helpful. detailed way that will allow the organisation to take legal action against individuals perpetrating fraud and corruption. It's a true game-changer for whistleblowers who usually walk the road of coming forward alone and risk losing their livelihoods and sometimes even their lives. OUTA will follow their cases every step of the way and make sure that perpetrators are made examples of. Using the example of Zwai Sokupa (who is speaking to us on condition of anonymity) we show how his information is enabling OUTA to blow the lid off corruption in a key development parastatal, and how they will continue to support whistleblowers financially and legally who help them reach their aim of safeguarding taxpayers' money. But OUTA's initiative is limited to the parastatals where their investigations are focused -- for the moment ESKOM and SAA, although this will change as they get good information on other state owned enterprises. So the broader legal landscape still remains crucial to challenge, as the Amendment Bill will do -- to afford whistelblowers true protection. So, the final initiative is by the Open Democracy Advice Centre itself -- the NGO that's been working with whistleblowers since the dawn of democracy and that's been working to change policy through research and advocacy, because it believes effective whistleblowing mechanisms are a key part of good governance. ODAC counsels and guides whistleblowers who come forward to bodies like Corruption Watch or the Public Protector, to guide them through the complex legal, emotional, psychological and often physically hazardous process of blowing the whistle. Now, hoping to take whistleblowing to the next level, and making the new law practical, helping to implement it, ODAC is launching a CODE of good practice and taking it around the country, to government departments and companies alike, to help them implement the new legislation and help make the world safe for whistleblowers. ODAC has held the hands of families like Tlholo Phakoe's whose father Moss was gunned down in 2009 after a lengthy period of tying to raise serious corruption issues in Madibeng, North West with senior leaders of the ANC -- most notably President Zuma, whom he visited at home, with his damning dossier. The murder of Moss Phakoe remains unsolved, while COSATU and Corruption Watch still campaign behind the scenes today to have the prosecutions reopened. It was the case of Moss Phakoe that marked a change in whistleblowing -- not only could you get fired, you could die.
